name: Carla Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Carla, and thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the junior buyer at Loomhouse Textiles, a family-owned wholesaler of fabric, thread and haberdashery out near the rail yard. Mornings I go through the sales report, then I order bolts of cotton, zips and buttons from mills and importers. I haggle on price, check samples when they arrive, and argue with the shipping agent about delays. I've only had this seat for four years, after a long time in warehouse packing, so I'm still learning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI in the job at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the samples. Some mornings it feels like Christmas, with new prints in boxes. What wears me out is the margin squeeze, because online marketplaces sell cheaper than our own customers can, and Mr Brandt (the owner) passes that pressure straight down to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the tools are handy and nothing more, and I'd keep using mine. To friends I'd say a lot of people oversold this. Online I'd post a joke about the chatbot ordering me 400 buttons by mistake, which it nearly did once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, it's fine for my job. AI already writes my supplier emails and checks my price comparisons every day. If nothing bigger happens, I'm still here, with the same low pay and the same no-savings problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and get a bit faster, so Mr Brandt sees I'm worth keeping. I'd ask for a small raise after my next review, with proof of what I've saved the firm. And I'd start a little side stall selling remnant fabric online on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady. I wouldn't call it exciting. I'm not scared, but I'm also aware that the pay is what it is and there's no buffer, so I'm never fully relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the side stall. How much could that bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joyce in dispatch says I'm the only one who isn't worried about the screens. I tell her they only help if you're willing to ask them the right questions. I've started showing her how to make the system flag late deliveries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen at Loomhouse if one of your big customers went under?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd worry about in a plateau is Loomhouse itself. Margins are tight, and one big customer going under could hurt us more than any software.

say: I'd say the tools are **handy**, nothing more, and I'd keep using mine.
I'd post a joke about the chatbot nearly ordering **400 buttons** by mistake.
think: The job is **fine** for me, since AI already does my supplier emails and price checks.
I'm still on **low pay** with no savings, so I never fully relax.
do: **Ask** for a small raise at my next review, with proof of what I've saved.
**Start** a weekend side stall selling remnant fabric online.
feel: **Steady** but never fully relaxed, with no buffer behind me.
S0.quote: AI already writes my supplier emails and checks my price comparisons every day.
fieldNote: She is the most at ease with the tools, yet money keeps her from calm.
Her risk is the **firm**, not the software: thin margins at a family business.
Shows initiative with a side stall and a raise case built on evidence.

steps.text: Ask for a small raise with proof of savings from my AI checks
Start selling fabric remnants online on weekends
Carry on ordering cotton and haberdashery from the same mills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd tell Mr Brandt that we should lead and not wait. To friends I'd say it's a real change but one you can ride if you're curious. Online I'd share tips, because I think the more people who know how to use these tools, the fairer it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, buying is exactly what the card names, so I know I'm in the firing line. The tools can already compare prices, chase orders and spot late shipments. I think the desk shrinks, and the question is whether I'm the one who's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person who sets up the tools for Loomhouse, so I'm useful beyond the order screen. I'd take an evening course in data basics, which the council subsidises. And I'd grow the side stall, because a second income would calm me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting and scary at once. I like learning, and I know I can keep up. But at 58 with no savings, the exciting part has a limit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter Defne about her own work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Defne, my daughter, designs packaging for a small brand, and she's already using AI to draft concepts. I'd tell my daughter to be the one who directs the machine and not the one who competes with it. It's what I'm trying to do myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if being quick with the tools still isn't enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The risk is that being quick isn't enough if the owners just decide to save money. If Mr Brandt cut the desk, there would be no jobs like mine nearby. I'd then have to move on to anything, even packing work again.

say: I'd tell Mr Brandt we should **lead** and not wait.
I'd share tips online, because the more people know the tools, the **fairer** it is.
think: Buying is exactly what the card names, so I'm in the **firing line**.
I think the desk shrinks, and the question is whether I'm still **there**.
do: **Become** the person who sets up the AI tools for Loomhouse.
**Take** the council-subsidised evening course in data basics.
**Grow** the weekend fabric stall into a second income.
feel: **Exciting and scary** at once, with a limit because I have no savings.
S1.quote: I'd tell my daughter to be the one who directs the machine and not the one who competes with it.
fieldNote: She **leans in** and plans to be the in-house expert, which is her best protection.
Anxious because her desk may shrink and local buying jobs are few.
Gives advice to her daughter that mirrors her own survival plan.

steps.text: Set up and look after the AI ordering tools for Loomhouse
Take the evening data-basics course the council subsidises
Grow the fabric remnant stall into steady weekend income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not a drill and we should treat it like one. At work I'd push Mr Brandt to talk about it openly. With friends I'd say governments and employers must pay people through the change, and I'd back whoever argues for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I can use the tools, but if they do everything better than me, so what? There'd be nothing left for a buyer to add. Two years is far too short for a 58-year-old with no savings to build something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the obvious things fast. I'd cut spending to the bone, put every spare pound into the account, and push the side stall harder. I'd also write to my MP and join the local branch of the union, because I think this one needs people acting together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a mix. There's a bit of a thrill, because I've been waiting to see this happen. There's a lot of fear too, and I'd say the fear wins when I think of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Stefan manage on one wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Stefan works as a bus mechanic, so his job is safe for a while. I'd tell him we might live on his pay alone if mine goes. We'd drop the car, the phone contract and the cable, and I'd rather tell my partner Stefan we might live on one wage, calmly now, than in a panic later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your colleagues, and would they listen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The one thing I'd do differently from my colleagues is not hide it. Joyce and the others would pretend nothing is happening. I'd tell them straight and ask us all to talk to Mr Brandt together.

say: I'd say it's **not a drill** and we should treat it like one.
I'd push Mr Brandt to talk about it **openly** with the team.
think: If the tools do everything better than me, there's **nothing left** for a buyer to add.
Two years is **far too short** to build something new with no savings.
do: **Cut** spending to the bone and save every spare pound.
**Push** the side stall harder and write to my MP.
**Join** the local union branch so we act together.
feel: A mix of **thrill** and fear, with the fear winning when I think of rent.
S2.quote: I'd rather tell my partner Stefan we might live on one wage, calmly now, than in a panic later.
fieldNote: She is adaptive but still **alarmed**: skills can't offset thin money in a two-year window.
Wants colleagues to confront it openly; it is her way of staying in control.
Plans for Stefan's wage to carry the household, so the cuts are specific.

steps.text: Drop the car, the phone contract and cable to live on Stefan's pay
Put every spare pound into the savings account
Push the fabric remnant stall to sell every weekend
Join the local union branch and ask colleagues to speak to Mr Brandt together

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's early enough to use well. At work I'd propose a plan to Mr Brandt for what Loomhouse does with the time. With friends I'd say we need real retraining, not a leaflet, and I'd ask politicians what they intend to pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years feels workable for me. I'd be 63, so I'd either have moved to work that's harder to automate or squeezed in a decent savings pot. Where it gets hard is that my savings today are close to zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year on a plan. I'd get a certificate in logistics or supply planning, which is thinking work with some hands-on parts. I'd build the stall into something real, and I'd save 150 a month. At 63, I might also look at part-time work as a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like being handed a map. I'd still be nervous, but at least I'd have some roads to choose between. Compared to the two-year one, I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What difference does having five years make compared to two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots coming three years after is interesting for me. My old warehouse job might be safe a bit longer. I'd rather not go back to packing, but if the choice is that or nothing, I'd take it for those extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really go back to warehouse work, and what would that feel like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to bet, I'd say I'd land on my feet because I'm willing to move, learn and look foolish. The people who'd struggle are the ones who say they'll wait and see.

say: I'd propose a **plan** to Mr Brandt for how Loomhouse uses the time.
I'd tell friends we need **real retraining**, not a leaflet.
think: Five years feels **workable** for me, though my savings today are close to zero.
I'd be 63 and either in harder-to-automate work or with a decent **pot**.
do: **Earn** a certificate in logistics or supply planning.
**Save** 150 a month and build the stall into a real business.
**Consider** part-time work at 63 as a bridge.
feel: Like being handed a **map**, with several roads to choose from.
S3.quote: I'd rather not go back to packing, but if the choice is that or nothing, I'd take it for those extra years.
fieldNote: Time gives her a plan, but savings near zero keep her at anxious.
She treats the three-year robot delay as a **fallback**: warehouse work as a bridge.
Self-aware about her strength, which is willingness to look foolish and learn.

steps.text: Earn a certificate in logistics or supply planning
Save 150 a month starting next payday
Turn the fabric remnant stall into a real online shop
Go back to warehouse packing for a few years if the desk goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. At work I'd tell Mr Brandt that Loomhouse could be first in the trade to use these tools well. With friends I'd say don't panic, but don't be lazy either, because ten years goes fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be about 68 when AGI lands, so I'd probably be retired or close to it. The tools make me more useful until then, so I feel fairly safe. My money is the only thing pulling me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep growing the stall and save steadily for the next six or seven years. I'd stay the person at work who knows the tools, so I'm the last to go. And I'd help Defne and my son Kerem plan, because they have most to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long, slow tide. I'm comfortable with it, and a bit curious. There's some sadness too, about what my grandchildren's world might look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son Kerem about his apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kerem is an apprentice electrician, so he'd have an extra three years before robots reach hands-on work, and I'd tell him to build skills in repair and installation, which are harder for robots. I'd tell Defne to learn how to direct AI, not compete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good outcome look like for you at 65?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, the thing I'd do with ten years is rest easier. I'd aim to leave work at 65 with a small pot and a side income, and I'd call that a good outcome for someone who started with nothing.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**, and Loomhouse could be first in the trade to use the tools well.
I'd tell friends not to panic and **not to be lazy** either.
think: I'd be about 68 when AGI lands, so I'd likely be **retired** or close.
My **money** is the only thing pulling me down.
do: **Grow** the stall and save steadily for six or seven years.
**Stay** the person at work who knows the tools.
**Help** my children Defne and Kerem plan their careers.
feel: Like a **long, slow tide**, with some curiosity and some sadness for my grandchildren.
S4.quote: I'd aim to leave work at 65 with a small pot and a side income, and I'd call that a good outcome for someone who started with nothing.
fieldNote: With a decade, she feels **useful** until retirement and mainly worries about money and her children.
Her advice to Kerem uses the three-year robot gap sensibly.
Ends with a modest, concrete goal: a small pot and a side income.

steps.text: Keep growing the stall and save steadily for six or seven years
Put a fixed amount into savings each month until 65
Stay the first person at Loomhouse to learn each new AI tool
Help Kerem plan his electrician apprenticeship and Defne her design work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no way I'd have a cushion built in time. I'm good with the tools, but thin savings and 58 are a bad pair. If it all goes in two years, I'd be scrambling with a head start but no runway.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say the people who are good with change still need a safety net. Being adaptable doesn't pay the rent. Please don't let anyone say 'just learn the tools' as if that's the whole answer.

headlineQuote: Being adaptable doesn't pay the rent. Please don't let anyone say 'just learn the tools' as if that's the whole answer.
portrait: Carla is 58, a junior buyer at **Loomhouse Textiles**, a family fabric wholesaler, with a partner and two grown children.
She is **adaptive** and uses AI every day, but her low pay and near-zero savings limit what skill can protect.
She is a **progressive** who blames big marketplaces and wants employers and government to share the cost of change.
Her mood rises and falls with the clock: **alarmed** at two years, anxious at five, uneasy at ten.
Her plan is the same each time: become the tools expert, grow her side stall, save, and look after her children.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because her cushion is near zero and two years is too short to build one.
whatWouldHelp: A real **safety net** while she retrains, and employers who pay for it rather than telling people to learn the tools.
